title: On a variance associated with the distribution of general sequences in arithmetic progressions. II
venue: Phil. Trans. R. Soc. Lond. A 356 (1998), no. 1738, 793–809
why: This is ref. [7] of Vaughan 2005. It gives Montgomery–Hooley-type asymptotics for general sequences that are approximately distributed in every residue class, not only the reduced ones, which is the situation for squarefree numbers. Its Theorem 1.2 and hypothesis (1.12) are what Vaughan 2005 sharpens. It is the template for the 'classical' route, with error at least x^{1+1/k} log x, and for the structure of the main term x^2 F(x/Q).

title: On a variance associated with the distribution of general sequences in arithmetic progressions. I
venue: Phil. Trans. R. Soc. Lond. A 356 (1998), no. 1738, 781–791
why: This is ref. [10] of Brüdern–Wooley. It is the circle-method treatment of the Montgomery–Hooley variance for general sequences equidistributed in reduced classes. Brüdern–Wooley say their major-arc treatment, with auxiliary averages of multiplicative functions, mirrors this paper.

authors: D. A. Goldston and R. C. Vaughan
title: On the Montgomery–Hooley asymptotic formula
venue: Sieve Methods, Exponential Sums, and their Applications in Number Theory (Cardiff, 1995), LMS Lecture Note Ser. 237, Cambridge Univ. Press (1997), 117–142
why: Origin of the method: the variance is reduced to counting n1 − n2 = hq with q ≤ Q and evaluated by the circle method, the minor arcs being handled through the product hq. Brüdern–Wooley adapt exactly this to n1 − n2 = h f(k). Page 118 has historical comments on the method. The DOI in the URL was not verified; check the landing page.

title: On a variance associated with the distribution of primes in arithmetic progressions
why: Ref. [11] of Brüdern–Wooley. A refined circle-method analysis of the prime variance with an explicit secondary main term. It is useful for how to extract the lower-order main terms from major arcs and singular-series-type averages.

authors: H. Mikawa and T. P. Peneva
title: Primes in arithmetic progressions to spaced moduli
why: The Barban–Davenport–Halberstam upper bound for primes with moduli f(k), weighted by f'(k) or k^{-1}φ(f(k)). This is the sparse-moduli predecessor that Brüdern–Wooley sharpen to an asymptotic, and a model for the upper-bound (BDH) part of the squarefree problem.

title: Square-free numbers in arithmetic progressions
why: First BDH/Montgomery–Hooley-type result for squarefree numbers, summing over all residue classes mod q (not only coprime ones), as in the present problem. Caution: Vaughan 2005 (p. 574) says the argument leading to Croft's (6.6) is faulty and the constant B in his (7.2) is wrong. Use it for structure only, not for constants.

title: Squarefree numbers in arithmetic progressions
why: Gives V(x,Q) = x^2 F(x/Q) + O(x^{3/2}(log x)^{7/2}) for squarefree numbers with F(y) = c y^{-3/2} + O(...), avoiding Croft's error. This is the classical benchmark main term c x^{1/2} Q^{3/2} for all moduli, against which the sparse main term should be checked.

title: On squarefree numbers in arithmetic progressions
why: Early variance and BDH-type bounds for squarefree numbers in progressions; cited by both Vaughan 2005 and BGPVW. The DOI was not verified; check via EuDML/GDZ, where Monatshefte scans of this era are often freely available.

title: Über quadratfreie Zahlen in arithmetischen Progressionen
why: A short follow-up improving the squarefree variance bounds; ref. [9] of Vaughan 2005.

title: Remainder estimates for squarefree integers in arithmetic progression
why: Mean-square and individual remainder estimates for Q(x;q,l) (from Orr's 1969 Syracuse thesis under Richert). Halberstam remarked that it is hard to improve upon. A source of elementary bounds for E(x;q,l) uniform in q and l. The DOI was not verified; older JNT volumes are in Elsevier's open archive.

title: A note on square-free numbers in arithmetic progressions
why: An individual bound for E(x;q,l), improving Prachar, which gives an asymptotic for Q(x;q,l) for q up to about x^{2/3−ε}. Useful for disposing of moduli f(k) in ranges where pointwise bounds suffice, and for the trivial estimate of the variance.

title: Über die kleinste quadratfreie Zahl einer arithmetischen Reihe
why: The classical elementary asymptotic Q(x;q,l) = g(q,l)x + O(x^{1/2}q^{-1/4}+q^{1/2+ε}) type for squarefree numbers in a progression. It is the simplest pointwise input. EuDML lists the full text via the Göttingen digitisation centre (GDZ).

title: Note on an asymptotic formula connected with r-free integers
why: Asymptotics for Σ μ_r(n+k_1)…μ_r(n+k_s) (r-free tuples) with error x^{2/(r+1)+ε}; cited by BGPVW. A k-free analogue of the shifted-correlation input. The DOI was not verified.

title: The square sieve and consecutive square-free numbers
why: Improves the error term for Σ μ²(n)μ²(n+1) to x^{7/11+ε} via the square sieve. Relevant if the team uses correlations of μ² with shifts; it shows the limits of the elementary error term. EuDML (doc 163852) lists it, likely with GDZ full text.

authors: J. Brüdern, A. Perelli and T. D. Wooley
title: Twins of k-free numbers and their exponential sum
why: L1 and L2 bounds for exponential sums over k-free twins, extending BGPVW's estimates for Σ μ_k(n)e(nα). Useful for minor-arc and mean-value bounds involving μ². Wooley's site lists a copy (math.purdue.edu/~twooley/publ/2000ktwin.pdf), but the fetch failed, so it is not verified. The page range is from memory: the search snippet showed 173–177, which looks truncated, so verify it.

title: Goldbach numbers in sparse sequences
why: Ref. [1] of Brüdern–Wooley: a circle-method treatment of additive problems along sparse sequences, including polynomial-value-type sets. Brüdern–Wooley borrow from it for handling sums over f(k) on major and minor arcs. The open Numdam/Centre Mersenne PDF was confirmed as a 1.6 MB AIF 48(2) p. 353 file.

title: On the Barban–Davenport–Halberstam theorem. I
why: Hooley's refinement of Montgomery's asymptotic, V(x,Q) = Qx log Q + cQx + O(...), via an elementary divisor-switching method. It is the classical alternative to the circle method and the source of the second main term. EuDML links the full text at GDZ (free), but it was not downloaded.

title: On the Barban–Davenport–Halberstam theorem. II
why: Ref. [6] of Brüdern–Wooley: further refinement of the Montgomery–Hooley formula, including what happens when the residue-class sum is over all classes. Background only.

title: Primes in arithmetic progressions
why: The original asymptotic for the BDH variance of primes, by expanding the square and counting n1 ≡ n2 mod q. Gives the basic expansion that all later works follow. Michigan Math. J. is free on Project Euclid, but the PDF could not be fetched to confirm.

authors: J. B. Friedlander and D. A. Goldston
title: Variance of distribution of primes in residue classes
why: Variance for a single modulus q near x, with the explicit correction term; cited by Brüdern–Wooley. Background on behaviour when moduli are large relative to x (the range f(y) close to x).

title: Bombieri–Vinogradov type theorems for sparse sets of moduli
why: BV and BDH-type theorems for sparse sets of moduli, e.g. squares and polynomial values, via large sieve inequalities for sparse moduli. An alternative (large-sieve) route to the upper bound for V_f, and a source of the admissible range of f(y) relative to x.

title: An improvement for the large sieve for square moduli
why: A large sieve inequality Σ_{q≤Q} Σ_{a mod q²} |Σ a_n e(an/q²)|² with improved bounds. Relevant if the team bounds V_f(x,y) from above by a large sieve with polynomial moduli (squarefree indicator as the sequence).

title: The large sieve with sparse sets of moduli
venue: J. Ramanujan Math. Soc. 21 (2006) (venue from memory, unverified); preprint arXiv:math/0508417 (2005)
why: A general large sieve for sparse moduli that are well distributed in progressions (extending Wolke), applied to squares. Gives a general framework for moduli f(k).

title: On the distribution of the roots of polynomial congruences
why: Equidistribution of ν/n for roots ν of f(ν) ≡ 0 mod n, via exponential sums over roots. Needed when counting k ≤ y with f(k) ≡ 0 mod d (or f(k) in a class) with error terms uniform in d, as in the main-term evaluation Σ_k f'(k)·(arithmetic function of f(k)). The DOI was not verified.

title: On the number of solutions of polynomial congruences and Thue equations
why: Sharp uniform upper bounds for ρ(p^k), the number of roots of f mod p^k, in terms of degree and discriminant. These are needed to control ρ(m) and the multiplicative functions built from it on all prime powers, including primes dividing the discriminant. AMS JAMS back content is usually free, and a scan is hosted at uwaterloo.ca/pure-mathematics (s0894-0347-1991-1119199-x_0.pdf), but its content could not be confirmed by text extraction.

title: A note on polynomial congruences
venue: Recent Progress in Analytic Number Theory, Vol. 1 (Durham, 1979), H. Halberstam and C. Hooley (eds.), Academic Press, London (1981), 193–196
why: Bound ρ(p^k) ≤ d·p^{k/2}-type, more precisely in terms of the discriminant, for the number of roots of f mod p^k. A simpler alternative to Stewart for showing ρ is O(m^ε) and multiplicative sums over ρ converge.

title: Short sums of certain arithmetic functions
why: Upper bounds of the expected order for Σ_{k≤y} F(|f(k)|) with F submultiplicative, e.g. divisor functions of polynomial values. Handy for bounding error terms like Σ_k τ(f(k)) that arise when E(x;f(k),l) is estimated pointwise. Acta Math. is now open on Project Euclid (euclid.acta/1485891131), but the PDF could not be fetched to confirm.

title: On the sum Σ_{k=1}^x d(f(k))
why: Σ_{k≤x} d(f(k)) ≍ x log x for irreducible f. The elementary prototype for the divisor-of-polynomial-value bounds needed in error terms. The DOI was not verified.

title: The Hardy–Littlewood Method, 2nd edition
venue: Cambridge Tracts in Mathematics 125, Cambridge University Press (1997)
why: Standard reference cited by all three corpus papers: Weyl's inequality, major-arc approximations, and the complete exponential sums S(q,a) = Σ e(a f(x)/q) bounds (Hua) needed for sums over k of e(α h f(k)) on the minor arcs.

authors: E. C. Titchmarsh (revised by D. R. Heath-Brown)
title: The Theory of the Riemann Zeta-Function, 2nd edition
why: Vaughan 2005 uses §6.19 (Vinogradov–Korobov zero-free region and bound for 1/ζ) and §§3.12–3.13 for Lemma 2.1 (Σ_{n≤y,(n,q)=1} μ(n)) and for the exp(−c(log x)^{3/5}(log log x)^{−1/5}) error terms.

authors: H. L. Montgomery and R. C. Vaughan
title: Multiplicative Number Theory I. Classical Theory
venue: Cambridge Studies in Advanced Mathematics 97, Cambridge University Press (2007)
why: Background on Dirichlet series of multiplicative functions, Perron's formula and contour shifting. This is the technique for evaluating the auxiliary sums Σ_q h(q)·(stuff) whose generating function involves ζ(2s+…) as in Vaughan 2005 §6.

title: On a variance associated with the distribution of general sequences in arithmetic progressions. II
venue: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London A 356 (1738), 793–809
why: Develops variance asymptotics for sequences with residue-dependent local densities, including non-coprime residue classes. Vaughan’s supplied 2005 paper explicitly identifies its Theorem 1.2 as an earlier framework applicable to k-free numbers.

title: Squarefree numbers in arithmetic progressions
venue: Journal of the London Mathematical Society (2) 22 (1), 21–24
why: Gives an earlier asymptotic for the squarefree variance averaged over moduli. The supplied Vaughan paper specifically recommends its treatment as avoiding a flaw in Croft’s argument.

title: Square-Free Numbers in Arithmetic Progressions
venue: Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society (3) 30 (2), 143–159
why: A central early reference for mean-square distribution of squarefree numbers in progressions. Read with Vaughan’s correction: the contour argument leading to Croft’s equation (6.6), and consequently a stated constant, is faulty.

title: Remainder estimates for squarefree integers in arithmetic progression
why: Establishes squarefree analogues of average remainder estimates associated with Barban, Bombieri, Davenport, Halberstam and Gallagher. A useful source for preliminary mean-square bounds before extracting a sparse-modulus asymptotic.

authors: D. A. Goldston and R. C. Vaughan
title: On the Montgomery-Hooley asymptotic formula
venue: Sieve Methods, Exponential Sums, and their Applications in Number Theory, London Mathematical Society Lecture Note Series 237, Cambridge University Press, 117–142
why: Treats the off-diagonal part of variance directly as an additive problem through the circle method. Its singular-series summation and contour arguments are explicitly used in the supplied sparse-prime paper; distinguish unconditional arguments from those assuming GRH.

title: On a variance associated with the distribution of general sequences in arithmetic progressions. I
venue: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London A 356 (1738), 781–791
why: Develops the general-sequence Montgomery–Hooley method when small-modulus equidistribution concerns reduced residue classes. Its concluding singular-series calculation is specifically cited by the supplied Brüdern–Wooley paper.

title: The Hardy-Littlewood Method
venue: Second edition, Cambridge Tracts in Mathematics 125, Cambridge University Press
why: Provides polynomial exponential-sum estimates and the circle-method machinery needed for sparse polynomial moduli. The supplied Brüdern–Wooley paper explicitly uses Theorems 5.2 and 7.4 and the transference exercise in Chapter 2.

title: The average value of divisor sums in arithmetic progressions
why: Studies mean-square errors over residue classes for a fixed modulus, with extensions explicitly including k-free numbers. Investigate its estimates as possible inputs for controlling portions of the sparse variance.

title: On the number of solutions of polynomial congruences and Thue equations
venue: Journal of the American Mathematical Society 4 (4), 793–835
why: Contains bounds for the number of solutions of polynomial congruences, useful when estimating local root counts and Euler factors. Check the degree, discriminant and nondegeneracy hypotheses before applying these bounds to the chosen polynomial.

authors: H. Mikawa and T. P. Peneva
title: Primes in arithmetic progressions to spaced moduli
why: Proves average distribution results for widely separated moduli. The supplied Brüdern–Wooley paper invokes this work to remove small polynomial moduli and specifically identifies Section 2.2 as containing an important ingredient.

title: Bombieri-Vinogradov type theorems for sparse sets of moduli
why: Establishes Barban–Davenport–Halberstam and Bombieri–Vinogradov type bounds for well-distributed sparse sets, including square moduli. Its precise distribution hypotheses provide a useful checklist for any alternative large-sieve treatment of polynomial moduli.

title: On the large sieve with sparse sets of moduli
venue: Journal of the Ramanujan Mathematical Society 21 (3), 279–295
why: Gives a large-sieve inequality for arbitrary coefficient sequences when the moduli satisfy suitable progression-counting conditions. This makes it a potential tool for squarefree exponential sums without requiring prime-specific coefficients.

title: On the frequency of pairs of square-free numbers with a given difference
venue: Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society 55 (10), 936–939
why: Studies squarefree pair correlations at a prescribed shift, the basic objects arising after expanding the variance. Useful for understanding the local correlation factors, while uniformity in varying shifts must be checked separately.

title: On the Barban-Davenport-Halberstam theorem. I
venue: Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik 274/275, 206–223
why: A foundational refinement of the Montgomery variance asymptotic and an important source for the divisor-switching approach. Read to understand the method that the general-sequence and sparse-modulus papers subsequently adapt.

title: Primes in arithmetic progressions
why: The original asymptotic treatment of the prime variance underlying the Montgomery–Hooley framework. Provides the classical benchmark for separating diagonal and off-diagonal contributions.

title: On squarefree numbers in arithmetic progressions
why: An early source for average distribution estimates for squarefree numbers, cited by both supplied squarefree papers. Useful for tracing the preliminary mean-square estimates and their large-sieve origins.

title: Integer-Valued Polynomials
venue: Mathematical Surveys and Monographs 48, American Mathematical Society
why: A reference for the distinction between polynomials with integer coefficients and rational polynomials taking integer values. Relevant to checking modular periodicity and the interpretation of local root counts in the problem’s full stated generality.

title: An improvement for the large sieve for square moduli
why: Improves large-sieve bounds for arbitrary sequences sampled at fractions with square denominators. Particularly useful if the team first restricts the problem to square moduli; the proof combines Weyl sums, quadratic Gauss sums and exponential-integral estimates.

title: The distribution of sequences in arithmetic progressions
why: A short contemporary overview connecting prime-distribution mean values with general arithmetic sequences and squarefree numbers. Its references independently connect Orr, Warlimont and Croft’s then-developing work.

title: Goldbach numbers in sparse sequences
why: Develops exponential-sum methods for sequences thinner than polynomial-value sequences. The supplied Brüdern–Wooley paper points to this work when discussing extensions beyond polynomial moduli.

authors: J. B. Friedlander and D. A. Goldston
title: Variance of distribution of primes in residue classes
why: Studies refined prime-variance estimates and their connection with additive correlations and singular series. Useful methodological background for the supplied sparse-prime paper, with conditional estimates kept separate from unconditional inputs.
